title: Indian-Origin Woman, Friend Killed by Subway Train in Lower Manhattan
excerpt: Malaika Chitre, 24, of Dayton, New Jersey, and Navam Kaul, 24, of Sayreville, were struck by a southbound No. 4 train around 3:15 a.m. Sunday at the Spring Street station; police are investigating how they ended up on the tracks.
body:
• Malaika Chitre, 24, of Dayton, New Jersey, and her friend Navam Kaul, 24, of Sayreville, were struck by a southbound No. 4 train around 3:15 a.m. Sunday at Manhattan's Spring Street station and pronounced dead at the scene, according to the NYPD.
  • The train operator spotted the two on the tracks and tried the emergency brake but could not stop in time; about 100 passengers were evacuated onto the platform afterward.
  • A bystander video circulating on social media shows the two on the tracks moments before the train arrived; police are investigating how they got there.
  • Law-enforcement sources told the New York Post that investigators are examining whether intoxication played a role and have not ruled out suicide, though no note was found and police have confirmed no explanation.

What happened

Two young friends from New Jersey were killed early Sunday morning when they were struck by a subway train in Lower Manhattan after ending up on the tracks at the Spring Street station, according to the New York Police Department.

Malaika Chitre, a 24-year-old Indian-origin woman from Dayton, and Navam Kaul, 24, from Sayreville were on the tracks when a southbound No. 4 train approached around 3:15 a.m., the New York Post reported. The train operator told supervisors she saw the two and attempted to activate the emergency brake but could not stop in time. Officers called to the station found them on the tracks after they had been struck; both were pronounced dead at the scene. Around 100 passengers aboard the train were evacuated onto the platform, according to the New York Daily News.

A video recorded by a bystander and later shared on social media appears to show the two sitting on the tracks shortly before the train arrived.

Who they were

Chitre and Kaul both graduated from Rutgers University in 2024. Chitre earned a Bachelor of Science degree from the Rutgers-New Brunswick School of Arts and Sciences and worked as a quality operations specialist at Acadia Pharmaceuticals; she was also pursuing a doctorate in pharmacy at Temple University, according to IANS. Kaul attended Rutgers Business School from fall 2020 to spring 2024 and worked as a financial data analyst at Bloomberg, according to his LinkedIn profile cited by LatestLY. Rajnikant Pipalia, who told the Post his son was a friend of Kaul's, said Kaul's family had immigrated from Nepal and that the two had grown up in the same world — part of the same South Asian circle in New Jersey, celebrating the same festivals.

"We are saddened to learn of the tragic death of these two former students."

— Dory Devlin, assistant vice president of news and media relations, Rutgers University

Conflicting accounts, ongoing investigation

How the two came to be on the tracks remains unclear, and accounts differ. Law-enforcement sources cited by the New York Post said one of the two may have fallen or climbed onto the tracks, with the other apparently going down after — a version echoed by IANS, which reported that Chitre dove onto the tracks to try to save Kaul after he fell. The train operator, however, described seeing both a man and a woman sitting on the tracks, with the woman laughing and pulling the man toward her just before the collision, according to Times Now World.

Investigators are examining several possibilities, including whether the two were impaired, and police have not ruled out suicide, though no note was recovered. Chitre's family has criticized media speculation about the incident, saying some reports aired sensational claims without factual basis.

The diaspora angle

The deaths have shaken the South Asian community in the New York–New Jersey region, where both victims grew up and where their circles overlapped across school, college, and work. Beyond the grief, the episode is a reminder of how quickly unverified video and speculation travel online — the family's plea for restraint applies to everyone sharing the bystander footage or drawing conclusions before the NYPD investigation concludes.

What to watch next

NYPD detectives are continuing to investigate the circumstances that led the two onto the tracks, and transit officials will review the incident as part of routine safety procedures. The families have asked for privacy. Readers should treat early accounts as preliminary: with no confirmed explanation, the official findings will take time.

nri_angle: The deaths of two 24-year-old New Jersey friends — an Indian-origin woman and a Nepali-American man — have shaken the South Asian community in the New York region, where both grew up and graduated from Rutgers in 2024.
